rows.solution: Use the half-angle identity \(1 + \cos x = 2\cos^2\frac{x}{2}\), which turns the integrand into a standard form: \(\int\frac{dx}{1 + \cos x} = \int\frac{dx}{2\cos^2\frac{x}{2}} = \frac{1}{2}\int\sec^2\frac{x}{2}\,dx\). Since \(\int\sec^2\frac{x}{2}\,dx = 2\tan\frac{x}{2}\), this equals \(\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2\tan\frac{x}{2} + C = \tan\frac{x}{2} + C\). (The factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) from the identity is cancelled by the 2 the chain rule produces on integrating, which is why no \(\frac{1}{2}\) survives in the answer.)

rows.stem: The general solution of the differential equation \(x\,dy - y\,dx = 0\) is
rows.solution: The variables separate: \(x\,dy = y\,dx\), so \(\frac{dy}{y} = \frac{dx}{x}\). Integrating both sides gives \(\log|y| = \log|x| + \log k_1\), that is \(y = k_1 x\), which can be written as \(x = ky\) with \(k = \frac{1}{k_1}\). So the general solution is \(x = ky\). (The forms \(xy = k\) and \(\log y + \log x = k\) both say \(xy\) is constant, which solves \(x\,dy + y\,dx = 0\) — the equation with the opposite sign.)

rows.stem: Direction cosines of line \(x = y = 1 - z\) are
rows.solution: Write the line in symmetric form. From \(x = y = 1 - z\), put each expression equal to a parameter: \(x = y\) and \(z = 1 - x\), so \(\frac{x}{1} = \frac{y}{1} = \frac{z - 1}{-1}\). Its direction ratios are therefore \(<1, 1, -1>\), whose magnitude is \(\sqrt{1 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{3}\). Dividing each by \(\sqrt{3}\) gives the direction cosines \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}\). (The triple \(1, 1, 1\) cannot be a set of direction cosines at all, since \(1^2 + 1^2 + 1^2 = 3 \ne 1\).)

rows.stem: A relation R on set A = \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) defined as R = \(\{(1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2)\}\) is
rows.solution: Test the three properties in turn on \(R = \{(1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2)\}\) over \(A = \{1, 2, 3\}\). Reflexive would require \((1,1)\), \((2,2)\) and \((3,3)\) all to be in R; only \((2,2)\) is, so R is not reflexive. Symmetric requires that whenever \((a,b) \in R\) so is \((b,a)\): \((1,2)\) is paired with \((2,1)\), and \((2,2)\) is its own reverse, so R is symmetric. Transitive would require, from \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\), that \((1,1) \in R\) — it is not, so R is not transitive. Hence R is symmetric only.

rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2}\cos x & -\sin x \\ \sin x & \dfrac{1}{2}\cos x \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A + A' = I\), then value of \(x \in \left[\dfrac{-\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) is
rows.solution: Write down the transpose and add. With \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{2}\cos x & -\sin x \\ \sin x & \frac{1}{2}\cos x \end{bmatrix}\), we have \(A' = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{2}\cos x & \sin x \\ -\sin x & \frac{1}{2}\cos x \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A + A' = \begin{bmatrix} \cos x & 0 \\ 0 & \cos x \end{bmatrix}\) — the off-diagonal terms cancel. Setting this equal to \(I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) gives \(\cos x = 1\), and the only value of \(x\) in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) with \(\cos x = 1\) is \(x = 0\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.solution: Differentiate \(e^{x + y} = 3x\) implicitly with respect to \(x\), remembering that \(y\) is a function of \(x\): \(e^{x + y}\left(1 + \frac{dy}{dx}\right) = 3\). Hence \(1 + \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3}{e^{x + y}}\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3}{e^{x + y}} - 1 = \frac{3 - e^{x + y}}{e^{x + y}}\).

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Find the co-ordinates of foot of perpendicular drawn from (0, 0, 0) to line \(\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y + 1}{-1} = \dfrac{z - 3}{-2}\).
rows.solution: Let the foot of the perpendicular be Q. Writing \(\frac{x}{1} = \frac{y + 1}{-1} = \frac{z - 3}{-2} = \lambda\), a general point of the line is \(Q\left(\lambda,\; -\lambda - 1,\; 3 - 2\lambda\right)\). With \(P(0, 0, 0)\), the vector \(\vec{PQ}\) has direction ratios \(<\lambda,\; -\lambda - 1,\; 3 - 2\lambda>\), while the line has direction ratios \(<1, -1, -2>\). Since \(PQ\) is perpendicular to the line, the dot product vanishes: \(1(\lambda) - 1(-\lambda - 1) - 2(3 - 2\lambda) = 0\), that is \(\lambda + \lambda + 1 - 6 + 4\lambda = 0\), so \(6\lambda = 5\) and \(\lambda = \frac{5}{6}\). Substituting back, the foot of the perpendicular is \(\left(\frac{5}{6},\; -\frac{11}{6},\; \frac{4}{3}\right)\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Functions in Parametric Form
rows.stem: If \(x = \sin t - \cos t\), \(y = \sin t \cos t\), find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \(t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
rows.solution: Differentiate each coordinate with respect to \(t\): \(\frac{dx}{dt} = \cos t + \sin t\), and by the product rule \(\frac{dy}{dt} = \cos t \cdot \cos t + \sin t \cdot (-\sin t) = \cos^2 t - \sin^2 t\). Hence \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\cos^2 t - \sin^2 t}{\cos t + \sin t} = \frac{(\cos t - \sin t)(\cos t + \sin t)}{\cos t + \sin t} = \cos t - \sin t\), the cancellation being legitimate near \(t = \frac{\pi}{4}\), where \(\cos t + \sin t = \sqrt{2} \ne 0\). At \(t = \frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{4} = \sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 0\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following linear programming problem graphically :

Maximize \(Z = 8000x + 12000y\)

Subject to constraints

\(3x + 4y \leq 60\)

\(x + 3y \leq 30\)

\(x \geq 0, y \geq 0\)
rows.solution: First find the corner points of the feasible region. The line \(3x + 4y = 60\) meets the axes at \((20, 0)\) and \((0, 15)\); the line \(x + 3y = 30\) meets them at \((30, 0)\) and \((0, 10)\). Solving the two together: from the second, \(x = 30 - 3y\), and substituting into the first, \(3(30 - 3y) + 4y = 60\), so \(-5y = -30\), giving \(y = 6\) and \(x = 12\). With \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\) the region is bounded, with corner points \(O(0, 0)\), \(A(0, 10)\), \(B(12, 6)\) and \(C(20, 0)\) — note that on the y-axis the binding constraint is \(x + 3y \le 30\), giving 10 rather than 15, and on the x-axis it is \(3x + 4y \le 60\), giving 20 rather than 30. Evaluating \(Z = 8000x + 12000y\) at each corner: \(Z(O) = 0\), \(Z(A) = 1{,}20{,}000\), \(Z(B) = 96{,}000 + 72{,}000 = 1{,}68{,}000\), \(Z(C) = 1{,}60{,}000\). Hence the maximum value is \(Z = 1{,}68{,}000\), attained at \(x = 12\), \(y = 6\).

Split the numerator into a multiple of the derivative of the quadratic plus a constant. Since \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(6x + x^2\right) = 6 + 2x\), write \(2x + 1 = A(6 + 2x) + B\); comparing coefficients of \(x\) gives \(2A = 2\), so \(A = 1\), and then \(6 + B = 1\) gives \(B = -5\). Hence \(I = \int\frac{6 + 2x}{\sqrt{6x + x^2}}\,dx - 5\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{6x + x^2}}\). For the first integral put \(u = 6x + x^2\), so \(du = (6 + 2x)dx\) and it becomes \(\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{u}} = 2\sqrt{u} = 2\sqrt{6x + x^2}\). For the second, complete the square: \(6x + x^2 = (x + 3)^2 - 3^2\), so \(\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x + 3)^2 - 3^2}} = \log\left|(x + 3) + \sqrt{6x + x^2}\right|\). Therefore \(I = 2\sqrt{6x + x^2} - 5\log\left|(x + 3) + \sqrt{6x + x^2}\right| + C\).

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.stem: Find the domain of \(p(x) = \sin^{-1}(1 - 2x^2)\). Hence, find the value of \(x\) for which \(p(x) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\). Also, write the range of \(2p(x) + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
rows.solution:
Domain. The domain of \(\sin^{-1}\) is \([-1, 1]\), so we need \(-1 \le 1 - 2x^2 \le 1\). The right-hand inequality gives \(-2x^2 \le 0\), which is true for every real \(x\); the left-hand one gives \(-2 \le -2x^2\), that is \(x^2 \le 1\), so \(-1 \le x \le 1\). Hence the domain of \(p\) is \([-1, 1]\).
Solving \(p(x) = \frac{\pi}{6}\). Here \(\sin^{-1}\left(1 - 2x^2\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}\), so \(1 - 2x^2 = \sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\). Then \(2x^2 = \frac{1}{2}\), so \(x^2 = \frac{1}{4}\) and \(x = \pm\frac{1}{2}\); both values lie in the domain, so \(x = \frac{1}{2}\) or \(x = -\frac{1}{2}\).
Range of \(2p(x) + \frac{\pi}{2}\). As \(x\) runs over \([-1, 1]\), the expression \(1 - 2x^2\) runs continuously over the whole of \([-1, 1]\) — it equals 1 at \(x = 0\) and \(-1\) at \(x = \pm 1\) — so \(p(x)\) takes every value in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\). Doubling gives \(-\pi \le 2p(x) \le \pi\), and adding \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) throughout gives \(-\frac{\pi}{2} \le 2p(x) + \frac{\pi}{2} \le \frac{3\pi}{2}\). Hence the required range is \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right]\).

rows.stem: Find the sub-interval of \((0, \pi)\) in which \(f(x) = \tan^{-1}(\sin x - \cos x)\) is increasing and decreasing.
rows.solution: Differentiate using the chain rule: \(f'(x) = \frac{\cos x + \sin x}{1 + (\sin x - \cos x)^2}\). The denominator is at least 1 and so is always positive, which means the sign of \(f'(x)\) is decided entirely by \(\cos x + \sin x\). Setting \(f'(x) = 0\) gives \(\cos x + \sin x = 0\), i.e. \(\tan x = -1\), whose only solution in \((0, \pi)\) is \(x = \frac{3\pi}{4}\). Writing \(\cos x + \sin x = \sqrt{2}\sin\left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) makes the sign easy to read: for \(x \in \left(0, \frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\) the angle \(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\) lies in \(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \pi\right)\), where the sine is positive, so \(f'(x) > 0\); for \(x \in \left(\frac{3\pi}{4}, \pi\right)\) it lies in \(\left(\pi, \frac{5\pi}{4}\right)\), where the sine is negative, so \(f'(x) < 0\). Hence \(f\) is increasing on \(\left(0, \frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\) and decreasing on \(\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}, \pi\right)\). (Since \(f'\) vanishes only at the single point \(x = \frac{3\pi}{4}\), the intervals may equally be quoted as \(\left(0, \frac{3\pi}{4}\right]\) and \(\left[\frac{3\pi}{4}, \pi\right)\).)

rows.stem: A rectangle of perimeter 24 cm is revolved along one of its sides to sweep out a cylinder of maximum volume. Find the dimensions of the rectangle.
rows.figure: DECORATIVE - a plain line drawing of a rectangle beside a cylinder with a rotation arrow, printed below the stem. It is unlabelled and carries no measurement; the perimeter and the axis of revolution are both stated in the text. Page idx 18. Not attached.
rows.solution: Let the sides of the rectangle be \(x\) and \(y\). The perimeter is 24 cm, so \(2(x + y) = 24\), giving \(y = 12 - x\) with \(0 < x < 12\). Revolve the rectangle about the side of length \(12 - x\); that side becomes the axis, so the cylinder swept out has height \(12 - x\) and radius \(x\). Its volume is \(V = \pi x^2 (12 - x) = \pi\left(12x^2 - x^3\right)\). Then \(\frac{dV}{dx} = \pi\left(24x - 3x^2\right) = 3\pi x(8 - x)\), which vanishes at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 8\); the value \(x = 0\) is rejected because it gives no cylinder at all, leaving \(x = 8\). Testing it, \(\frac{d^2V}{dx^2} = \pi(24 - 6x)\), and at \(x = 8\) this is \(\pi(24 - 48) = -24\pi < 0\), so the volume is indeed a maximum there. Hence \(x = 8\) and \(12 - x = 4\), so the dimensions of the rectangle are 8 cm and 4 cm. (Because \(x\) is free to take any value in \((0, 12)\), this single calculation already compares both ways of choosing the axis of revolution.)
